items.title: US authorities seize domains behind a China-based firm’s scanning tool whose targets included airports in Japan and Poland
items.content_text: On 8 October the Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains behind two tools: Microscan, a Python web application with more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts supported by a Mirai-variant IoT botnet, and FishHub, a spear-phishing and malware-delivery platform. US authorities say China-based Integrity Technology Group built and ran them; CyberScoop calls the tools Flax Typhoon-linked, while Cybersecurity Dive says the activity mimics that group. Court documents list Microscan targets including airports in Japan and Poland, a South Carolina power company and gas and power firms in Taiwan; FishHub went after Taiwanese universities. Neither report confirms that any airport was breached. A joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory, AA26-281A, describes scanning, cross-site scripting, Exchange password spraying and persistence through VPN software. It still leads this page: we found no newer development on the seizures as of 28 October, nothing reported since names aviation infrastructure, and we found no airport, airline or air traffic cyber incident dated 22 to 28 October.

items.title: Attackers took over refrigeration controllers at about 700 French supermarkets — a warning for every internet-reachable building controller on an airport estate
items.content_text: Over the nights of 11–13 October, attackers remotely changed settings on web-managed refrigeration controllers in French supermarkets, forcing long defrost cycles with temperatures reported as high as about 50°C, spoiling stock and, according to the Paris prosecutor, starting fires at some stores. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that about 700 of France’s roughly 10,000 supermarkets were affected, and Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché and Monoprix have confirmed impact. CERT-FR’s alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb on 13 October, and in its 16 October update, still the latest version as of 28 October, says the campaigns are probably still running; no new attack nights have been reported since 13 October. Danfoss and Copeland both say most affected units are older or end-of-life models. No group has claimed the attack, no ransom has been demanded and the entry route has not been established; the prosecutor’s cybercrime section has assigned the inquiry to OFAC, France’s anti-cybercrime office. This is not an aviation incident and it does not count toward this page’s threat level. Our assessment of why it is here: airport terminals, flight-catering units and cargo cold stores run the same class of remotely managed refrigeration and building controllers, often maintained by a contractor through a web interface, and this attack shows how directly a changed setpoint becomes physical loss.

items.title: FBI and Secret Service: the FortiBleed credential campaign against FortiGate VPNs is still running, and their advisory covers every critical-infrastructure sector, transportation included
items.content_text: On Tuesday 6 October the FBI and the US Secret Service issued joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01 warning that the FortiBleed campaign remains active: attackers are still scanning internet-facing Fortinet firewalls and SSL VPN gateways and logging in with credentials obtained earlier. There is no CVE. The agencies tie the campaign to reused or leaked passwords and legacy SHA-256 password storage; researchers describe password spraying and stuffing from leak dumps, offline cracking of extracted hashes and a sniffer that captures authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Some owners were locked out after the intruders created their own administrator accounts and deleted or reset the real ones. The access is resold, the FBI links it to Payload ransomware, and SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments from it. SOCRadar’s figure of more than 86,644 working device credentials in 194 countries dates from 19 June; it is not a new count. The advisory says it applies to all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors and names transportation systems among them, and Cybersecurity Dive reports that targeted organisations span every one of the 16. No OT system compromise has been described and no aviation victim is named. Our assessment: FortiGate is a common boundary device between airport and airline corporate networks and terminal and airfield systems, so a stolen admin login there is a stolen boundary.

items.title: Forescout finds almost 13,000 internet-exposed refrigeration management services in 99 countries — most of the Danfoss systems on old firmware
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published on 22 October a count of refrigeration controllers reachable from the internet, prompted by the attacks on French supermarkets over 11–13 October. Searching for ten product families, it found 12,976 exposed service observations on 6,017 public addresses in 99 countries and territories; the unit is services, not devices, because one address can expose several ports. Copeland and Dixell XWEB accounted for 7,075 observations, Danfoss StoreView for 4,697, Copeland Site Supervisor for 551 and CAREL pCOWeb for 513. About 80% of the Danfoss AK-SM 800A StoreView services ran firmware older than 4.3.1, which carries published flaws, and the original AK-SM 800 has been out of support since May 2021. Forescout says the entry route, exploited flaws and actor in the French attacks are still unknown. It also counts more than 20 attacks on refrigeration systems claimed by pro-Russian hacktivist groups since January 2026, mostly in Spain and Italy; those are claims, not confirmed incidents. Our assessment: airport food courts, flight-catering units and cargo cold stores, including pharmaceutical storage, use the same class of controller, usually installed and watched by a refrigeration contractor rather than the airport’s IT or OT team.

items.title: Two trackers, two August records: NCC Group counts 1,073 ransomware attacks and Comparitech 997 — and a newer group, Aurora, lists transportation among its targets
items.content_text: NCC Group’s review of August 2026, reported by Industrial Cyber on 28 September, counted 1,073 ransomware attacks, up 12% on July’s 960, which Industrial Cyber reports as a 2026 high. The industrial sector accounted for 329 attacks, about 31%; North America for 473, about 44%; and Europe for 276, about 26%. Qilin led with 164 attacks, about 15%, overtaking The Gentlemen, and DragonForce was also active. NCC also profiles Aurora, a ransomware-as-a-service group active since late April 2026 that targets manufacturing, legal, research and development and transportation organisations through weak or unauthenticated VPN access and PowerShell credential harvesting, then encrypts hypervisors. Comparitech, reported on 14 September, counted 997 attacks in August, a 23% rise on July’s 809 and above its previous monthly record of 988, with utility, healthcare and business-services attacks behind the rise. The two figures differ because the trackers count differently; both rest on leak-site claims and disclosures, a claimed victim is not a confirmed one, and neither describes confirmed OT downtime. For aviation the useful detail is Aurora’s way in. Weak VPN authentication is exactly the gap that integrator and contractor remote access into airports tends to leave, and encrypting the hypervisor takes down every virtual server on it at once — which is how a back-office ransomware event becomes a check-in, baggage or turnaround outage.

items.title: Nozomi’s summer telemetry puts transportation second for OT and IoT alerts per customer, behind only manufacturing
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs’ report on June to August 2026, published 12 October, ranks manufacturing first by alerts per organisation, transportation second, and energy, utilities and waste third, displacing government. About a third of detections involved credential-related techniques. Among alerts Nozomi attributes to a named actor, Scattered Spider accounted for close to half, and Russia-linked or Russian-speaking actors together for more than a third. Siemens PLCs and Rockwell products were among the vulnerable products detected most often, and Nozomi says 58% of the vulnerabilities published in 2026 rate High or Critical, against 48% in 2025. Read the numbers for what they are: alerts per customer across Nozomi’s own installed base, which measures detection activity, not confirmed attacks, and the report does not break transportation down by mode. For airports and airlines the useful signal is the weighting toward credentials, because accounts and logins are where integrator, handler and vendor access lives.

items.title: Dragos says old worms such as Conficker and WannaCry keep turning up in OT networks — and that a careless cleanup can do more harm than the infection
items.content_text: In a post published 15 October, Dragos’s Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff say requests for help with legacy commodity infections — Sality, Gammima, WannaCry and Conficker among them — have risen sharply in recent years. Many OT networks Dragos is called into carry 20 to 70 distinct commodity-malware variants spread across several subnets, often on machines older than Windows XP SP2. They attribute the rise to more networking and remote access, better visibility, and rules that require critical-infrastructure networks to be clean, and they set out a “Now / Next / Never” framework, with a white paper, for deciding what to remove and when. Their main warning is that a badly planned removal can cause more operational damage than the malware itself. Nothing here is a targeted campaign. Our assessment for this page: workstations that run baggage handling, airfield lighting and building management at airports often sit on old Windows builds that cannot be patched or rebooted on demand, so the same triage question applies before anyone runs a cleanup tool.

items.title: PHP2Shell is now in KEV, and Palo Alto reports attacks on internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces — including the PAN-OS that runs on Siemens’ RUGGEDCOM APE1808
items.content_text: CISA added both PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 26 October with a 29 October federal deadline. Perplexity’s Adel Karimi, with Expel’s Marcus Hutchins concurring, confirmed working remote code execution against a honeypot over 24–25 October. No victim organisation has been named, CISA did not describe the activity behind the listing, and Sophos and Palo Alto’s Unit 42 withdrew earlier reports of successful exploitation. The PHP Group rates both flaws CVSS v4.0 9.2 and fixed them on 21 October in PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and CISA published a SIGMA detection rule on 23 October; a third PHP flaw, CVE-2026-115560, has only a configuration mitigation and is not in KEV. For this page the firewall is the bigger story. Palo Alto’s product advisory, raised to Critical on 27 October and updated again on 28 October, says active exploitation has been observed targeting PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama are affected through the management web interface and XML API, and a dataplane interface only if it has a management profile attached; GlobalProtect portals and gateways, Prisma Access and Cloud NGFW are not. Palo Alto scores the issue CVSS v4.0 9.2, falling to 5.2 when management access is limited to a jump box. Hotfixes have shipped since 21 October, for example 12.2.4-h1, 11.1.16-h4 and 10.2.18-h13, while a few 10.2, 11.1, 11.2 and 12.1 hotfixes were still due on 29–30 October. The same hotfixes also fix the Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497, which CISA added to KEV on 27 October, except 11.2.10-h16. Siemens’ SSA-566512 lists RUGGEDCOM APE1808 devices running PAN-OS 10.2 to 12.2 as affected; customers get the patch through Siemens customer support and should apply Palo Alto’s workarounds meanwhile. Palo Alto names no victims, and no airport, airline or air navigation service provider has been named. Our assessment: PAN-OS firewalls commonly separate airport and airline corporate networks from terminal, baggage and airfield systems, so an internet-reachable management interface on one of them is the exposure to close first.

items.title: A three-flaw chain gives attackers root on fully patched Ivanti Connect Secure VPNs — one CVE is fixed and in KEV, the privilege-escalation link is not
items.content_text: Ivanti disclosed CVE-2026-104935 on 13 October: an authentication bypass in Connect Secure that, together with a file-write flaw, lets a remote unauthenticated attacker run commands (CVSS v3.1 8.6, Ivanti). Both flaws are fixed under that single CVE in 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2 and 25.1.3.0/25.1.3.1. A third bug, a privilege escalation in the dsinvoked broker, completes the chain to root; as of 28 October we still found no Ivanti fix for it; Volexity said on 13 October that one would come in the coming weeks. Volexity found the chain while responding to an intrusion and attributes it to a new actor it tracks as UTA0576. Exploitation began in early October — Volexity’s case dates from 3 October and Defused saw activity from 1 October — against an appliance that was fully patched at the time. The intruders left no web shell, ran commands through the exploit requests themselves, stole LDAP and domain credentials, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, Kerberoasted, sprayed passwords and wiped Ivanti debug and Linux audit logs. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 13 October with a 16 October deadline. CISA and Volexity warn that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect a compromise; Volexity says the chain patches library code in memory and restores configuration data, so a clean result is not proof. Ivanti says a limited number of customers were affected, and no aviation victim is named. Our assessment: Connect Secure is a common route into airline operations and engineering systems and for integrator access to terminal estates, and directory credentials taken through the VPN outlive the patch.

items.title: Citrix NetScaler: three zero-days exploited since late summer, and a fourth critical SAML flaw means some appliances patched last month need upgrading again
items.content_text: Citrix’s NetScaler ADC and Gateway have had three exploited zero-days in little more than a week. CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (each CVSS v4 9.5) were patched on 27 September in bulletin CTX697096 and added to KEV that day; CVE-2026-88779, which Citrix and watchTowr describe as a denial-of-service flaw affecting appliances configured as a SAML provider (CVSS v4 8.7, bulletin CTX697174), followed into KEV on 4 October. CISA has since warned that attackers use CVE-2026-88779 to force reboots so that code planted through CVE-2026-88771 runs. Google’s threat intelligence group traces the activity to at least 3 September and Palo Alto Networks to 21 August; Mandiant counts dozens of affected organisations across North America and Europe and describes actors with suspected state-nexus links, naming no group. Arctic Wolf’s figure of 78 counts targeted organisations, not confirmed compromises. On 8 October Citrix published CTX697191 for a fourth flaw, CVE-2026-107406 (CVSS v4 9.5), a memory overflow on appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider that Citrix says may lead to code execution or denial of service. It is not reported exploited and is not in KEV as of CISA’s 27 October catalog. The builds that fixed the September zero-days stay vulnerable to it when the appliance is a SAML identity provider, so those appliances must be upgraded again; fixed builds are 14.1-73.46 (including FIPS), 13.1-64.29 and, for FIPS/NDcPP, 13.1-37.283, or later. Shadowserver counts more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider has been named. Our assessment: NetScaler Gateway fronts crew and operations portals, MRO applications and integrator access into terminal systems, and as Mandiant has stressed, upgrading does not remove an intruder who is already in or recover stolen credentials.

items.title: Fortinet’s FortiMail has an exploited CVSS 9.8 flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker write files to the appliance — in KEV since 1 October, with fixed releases listed in Fortinet’s 5 October update
items.content_text: Fortinet published PSIRT advisory FG-IR-26-175 on 1 October for CVE-2026-104286 in its FortiMail email security gateway: a path traversal combined with improper handling of NULL bytes that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the underlying system with crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet scores it CVSS v3 9.8, says it has been reported as exploited in the wild, and found it internally. Affected releases are 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 1 October with a three-day federal deadline of 4 October, which has passed. When the advisory first appeared, fixed releases were planned but undated; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2, and tells 7.2 customers to move to the 7.4 branch or later. Fortinet’s workarounds are to disable Identity-Based Encryption (IBE), restrict webmail and management access to trusted networks, and use web-application-firewall rules that block POST requests containing ../ to /ibe paths. No actor, victim or targeted sector has been disclosed. This is not an OT product, and no airport or airline is named. Our assessment of why it is carried: a mail gateway is internet-facing by design, so at an airport authority, airline, ground handler or MRO an unauthenticated file-write flaw on it is a foothold on the corporate edge, and the corporate edge is where the paths into terminal and airfield systems begin.

items.title: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager has an exploited authentication bypass that gives an unauthenticated attacker administrator access — the controller that configures the links to outlying sites
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU on 30 September for CVE-2026-76504 in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, which Cisco rates CVSS 9.8. Improper handling of URI encoding lets a crafted request get past an authentication rule meant to restrict access to a particular API endpoint, giving a remote, unauthenticated attacker administrator-level access. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September 2026, and there are no workarounds. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1; anything older than 20.9 has to migrate to a fixed release. Cisco revised the advisory to version 1.1 on 2 October. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 30 September with a 3 October federal deadline, which has passed. BleepingComputer counts it as the fifth exploited Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. Cisco names no actor or victim, and no aviation organisation is named. Our assessment of the aviation angle is the same as for Arista’s VeloCloud Orchestrator: the SD-WAN manager is where configuration and policy for every edge router are set, and those edges can connect remote NAVAID and surveillance sites, fuel farms, cargo and MRO facilities and regional airports to the core network. Administrator access to the manager is a view of every site and possibly a way to change how traffic reaches each one.

items.title: MikroTik RouterOS: three exploited flaws in KEV, and now a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication web-management flaw from CISA that is not reported exploited
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-67279 in MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 25 September, with a federal deadline of 28 September. KEV describes it as improper enforcement of a behavioural workflow in SSH that “could allow an unauthenticated client to open a session channel and send an exec request,” and notes that it can be chained to exploit CVE-2026-86060 without authentication. Coverage rates it CVSS 6.9, with no scoring version stated. It joins two RouterOS flaws CISA added on 10 September: CVE-2026-86060, an argument-injection flaw, and CVE-2026-67277, a missing-authentication flaw in the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska’s posts of 5 September reported in-the-wild exploitation, from about 2 September, of a two-flaw SSH chain it calls “MikroTrick”. CERT Polska’s 22 September technical analysis names the chain: CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060, which gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. CVE-2026-67276, which earlier coverage tied to the chain, is not in KEV. Fixed builds are RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21; the related CVE-2026-67278 needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6, because the earlier fix was incomplete. Shadowserver counted more than 122,500 MikroTik devices with SSH reachable from the internet in early September; that is an exposure count, not a count of unpatched or compromised devices. No victims, sectors or actor have been named. The aviation relevance is breadth rather than any confirmed airport targeting: RouterOS boxes turn up in the inexpensive, quietly installed corners of an airport estate — remote stands and cargo sheds, car parks and shuttle depots, contractor site offices, CCTV and Wi-Fi backhaul — the places least likely to appear in an asset register and most likely to have an SSH port open for vendor support. Update, 29 September: CISA published ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 for a separate RouterOS flaw, CVE-2026-84411, a pre-authentication integer underflow in the web management interface that can lead to code execution or denial of service, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 9.3. RouterOS before 7.24 is affected, and CISA lists 7.24 or later as fixed. It is not in KEV, no exploitation has been reported, and it is not part of the chain CERT Polska named.

items.title: A CVSS 10 command-injection flaw in VIVOTEK camera firmware covers 37 models and already has public proof-of-concept code — CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors that use them
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-272-03 on 29 September for CVE-2026-22755, a command-injection flaw in VIVOTEK IP camera firmware affecting 37 camera models. It is rated CVSS v3.1 10.0 and v4 9.3, and public proof-of-concept code exists. The remedy is the latest firmware for each model. CISA lists Government Services and Facilities, Transportation Systems, Commercial Facilities, Energy, Critical Manufacturing and Financial Services among the sectors concerned, and reports no known exploitation. Nothing in the advisory names an airport. Our assessment of why it belongs here: IP cameras are among the most numerous networked devices on an airport estate, in terminals, car parks, cargo areas, aprons and along the perimeter, and they are usually installed and maintained by a security integrator rather than by IT. Public exploit code for a maximum-severity flaw shortens the time before someone scans for them, and a compromised camera is a foothold on the video network, which often shares cabling and switches with access control. The same 29 September batch of seven advisories also covered the Lantronix G520 cellular gateway, a new MikroTik RouterOS flaw, Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT terminal software, and three products for which no fix is planned: a Baicells LTE base station, an Anjvision product and the Viidure dashcam app.

items.title: Arista’s VeloCloud SD-WAN orchestrator has its third exploited zero-day in four months — now in KEV, and September’s fix does not cover it
items.content_text: Arista published Security Advisory 0199 on 22 October for CVE-2026-114625, a SQL injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), the console that pushes configuration and policy to every SD-WAN edge it manages. Any authenticated user, down to the Enterprise Read Only role, can gain operator privileges by posing as a local “superuser operator” account and reach functions meant only for internal use. Arista rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4, says it detected the activity itself and that the flaw is “known to be actively exploited”, and notes that VCO is exposed by default with no configuration that prevents it. Fixed releases are 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12; hosted and dedicated orchestrators have already been patched, and VeloCloud Edges and Gateways are not affected. It is the third exploited VCO zero-day since July, after CVE-2026-16812 and September’s CVE-2026-93952, so builds patched last month are still exposed. CISA added it to KEV on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, which has passed; no victim or actor has been named. Our assessment: SD-WAN edges often link remote navigation-aid and surveillance sites, fuel farms, cargo and MRO facilities and regional airports to the core network, so an attacker holding the orchestrator can see, and possibly reconfigure, every one of those links.

items.title: PHP2Shell and airport building systems: Siemens lists Desigo, Siveillance and SiPass as not affected, Schneider’s Security Expert has a fix and Control Engineering now has remediation
items.content_text: With the PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, now exploited and in KEV (see the PAN-OS card), the question for airport facilities and security teams is which of their building, security and control products bundle PHP. Siemens’ SSA-166980, published 26 October and updated 27 October, lists 20 Smart Infrastructure products as not affected because they do not contain PHP. They include Desigo CC, Desigo Optic and the Desigo PXC4, PXC5 and PXC7 automation stations; SiPass integrated and SIPORT access control; Siveillance Control, Control Pro, Intrusion and Video; the Sinteso FS20 EN fire-detection system; Climatix; Building X; and Connect X200, X300 and X500. Siemens says its evaluation is still under way and the findings may change; a separate notice, SSA-566435, lists 31 Siemens software products as not affected. Schneider Electric’s bulletin SESB-2026-295-01 names three affected products. EcoStruxure Security Expert, an access-control and security-management platform, is fixed in 1.48.4.0, and ProLeiT LINEoptimize is remediated through ProLeiT support. For EcoStruxure Control Engineering, version 2.0.0 of the bulletin, issued 26 October, says remediation is now available: it applies automatically when the system can reach the debian.org and sury.org repositories, and otherwise customers request a patch from Schneider. ABB and B&R list APROL up to R 4.4-65 as affected, with patches planned for 26 and 29 October, and ABB MES installations that include DokuWiki, where the fix is to update PHP or shut DokuWiki down; ABB scores both flaws CVSS v3.1 9.8. Rockwell Automation’s SD1802 of 23 October says no products have been confirmed affected and its review continues, and Moxa has published its own notice, MPSA-260001. No exploitation of these vendors’ own products has been reported. Our assessment: Security Expert and the Siemens building, fire and security lines are the kind of platforms that run terminal access control, intrusion detection and building management, so the not-affected list settles the first question for many airports; the remaining risk is integrator-built web front ends and dashboards that bundle PHP without documenting it.

items.title: Attackers are using a signed Siemens Software Center executable to load malware in a ClickFix campaign — CISA added the flaw to KEV on 20 October
items.content_text: Siemens confirmed on 19 October that CVE-2026-110936, an uncontrolled search path flaw (CWE-427) in Siemens Software Center, is being exploited in what it calls the “Romulus” multi-platform ClickFix campaign. The attackers pair a genuine, validly signed Software Center executable with their own DLLs, delivered in an installer named AllMyBasic.msi, so that the trusted program loads their code. Siemens says that, to its knowledge, no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached, and it names no final malware payload. It rates the flaw CVSS v3.1 6.7 and v4.0 8.4: the attacker needs local execution, which the ClickFix lure obtains by persuading a user to paste and run a command. Every version before V4.0.9.8 is affected; V4.0.9.8 fixes it, and existing installations update themselves on next start. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November federal deadline and on 22 October republished Siemens’ advisory as ICSA-26-295-03, listing Transportation Systems among the affected sectors. No aviation victim is named. Our assessment: for an airport or airline the risk lies in the signature more than the software. Application allowlisting on engineering and operations workstations often trusts Siemens-signed files, and as Siemens describes the chain the lure brings its own copy of the executable, so updating your own installations does not on its own stop it from running.

items.title: A suspected Chinese espionage group exploited a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day from late August; the fix shipped on 8 October and the flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: On 15 October Google’s threat intelligence group attributed zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, on the basis of overlapping tools and techniques. Exploitation began in late August. The flaw, rated CVSS v4 9.3 by BeyondTrust, lets attackers abuse the product’s internal messaging components to carry out file operations on Remote Support appliances; versions up to and including 26.2.3 are affected. BeyondTrust identified the defect in late September, shipped patch BT26-05-RS on 8 October and had patched its cloud-hosted customers by 9 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand, and releases older than 24.3.1 must be upgraded first. SecurityWeek reports that two appliances were compromised, one hosted by BeyondTrust and one self-hosted. The attackers gained root, installed the SAWFLY PHP web shell and the BARECLAW SOCKS5 tunneller, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the tool’s own file transfer to take documents from user desktops. Google names no victims for this activity. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline, which has passed. Our assessment: remote-support tools of this kind are how many IT providers and integrators reach airport and airline workstations, including machines that sit beside operational systems.

items.title: Intruders who took over a provider’s FortiManager reached more than 500 managed FortiGates — the FortiOS flaw they used for root is now in KEV
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 14 October an intrusion at a telecommunications managed-service provider. The attackers got in through CVE-2024-47575 in FortiManager, the console the provider used to run its customers’ firewalls, then used CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS command-line path traversal, to gain root on managed FortiGates and install the PEERSTITCH loader with an SSH reverse-shell back door. Configurations, serial numbers and public addresses of more than 500 managed FortiGates were taken; Unit 42 describes this as exposure of configuration and credential material, not confirmed intrusion into the customers’ networks. It tracks the activity as CL-STA-0954, also known as UNC5820, which overlaps with suspected nation-state intrusions, but it names no state. Fortinet fixed CVE-2025-61624 in April under FG-IR-26-122, rates it Medium because it needs privileged, authenticated access, and now marks it known exploited. CISA added it to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October deadline. The CVE record also lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, which runs FortiOS. Our assessment: many airports and airlines have a provider run their firewalls through FortiManager, so this is a question to put to that provider as much as a patch to apply.

items.title: Palo Alto Networks fixes a PAN-OS zero-day that lets an authenticated attacker on the management interface run code as root — in KEV since 14 October
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks disclosed CVE-2026-0322 on 14 October: a code-injection flaw that lets an authenticated attacker with network access to the PAN-OS management interface execute code as root on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama, with no special configuration required. The company found it internally, reports very limited exploitation aimed at the management interface and has published three US-based IP addresses tied to the attempts; it names no actor or timeline. Prisma Access and Cloud NGFW are not affected. Palo Alto scores it CVSS v4 8.6 for network access. Fixed releases include 12.2.4, 12.1.10-h2, 11.2.16, 11.1.16-h3 and 10.2.18-h12, with hotfixes for other branches. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 17 October deadline. Separately, ReliaQuest warned on 9 October that Qilin and Settra ransomware operators are exploiting CVE-2026-0257, the older GlobalProtect authentication bypass Palo Alto disclosed in May, and that fixing it may not undo access gained before the patch. No aviation victim is named for either flaw. Our assessment: PAN-OS firewalls often sit on the boundary between airport or airline corporate networks and terminal and airfield systems, so root on the firewall means control of that boundary’s rules. The same management interface is now also being attacked through the PHP2Shell flaws (see that card).

items.title: Attackers began probing SonicWall’s CVSS 10 SMA1000 flaw within two days of the fix; no successful breach has been confirmed
items.content_text: SonicWall published advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 with hotfixes on 6 October for CVE-2026-102255, a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the SMA1000 WorkPlace interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker make the appliance send requests to its own internal functions. CISA’s enrichment scores it CVSS v3.1 10.0 and SonicWall calls it maximum severity. Three authenticated flaws were fixed alongside it: an OS command injection, a Zip Slip in the management console and a stored cross-site scripting bug. Affected are SMA 6210, 7210 and 8200v appliances on 12.4.3-03526 or older and 12.5.0-02952 or older; fixed builds are 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082. SMA 100 and firewall SSL VPN are not affected, and there is no workaround. Defused recorded the first hits on its decoy appliances on 8 October and Previdian logged 135 attempts from two US addresses. Reporting so far describes attempts, not confirmed compromises, and the flaw is not in KEV as of CISA’s 27 October catalog; some vulnerability feeds mark it exploited, but no confirmation has been published. SMA1000 appliances have been exploited repeatedly during 2026. Our assessment: SMA1000 is often the box through which vendors and integrators reach customer networks, which on an airport estate can include baggage, BMS and access-control systems.

items.title: Mitsubishi Electric fixes an authentication bypass across ICONICS GENESIS64 and GENESIS — MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz will not be fixed
items.content_text: Mitsubishi Electric’s advisory 2026-006 of 15 October covers the ICONICS SCADA, HMI and analytics family. The most serious network-reachable flaw, CVE-2026-16436 (CVSS v4.0 9.2), is a weak password-recovery mechanism: the challenge response that unlocks the system is fixed and shared by all users, so anyone who obtains it, including a remote attacker, can unlock the system. CVE-2026-16438 (v4.0 9.4) comes from installers that give the product’s administrator account unnecessary default DCOM permissions, letting that account launch DCOM objects locally or remotely without UAC elevation. CVE-2026-16437 (v4.0 7.1) lets a local administrator tamper with the challenge-response file, and the bundled libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (v4.0 9.3) affects GENESIS64 10.97 to 10.97.2 when an administrator imports a crafted file. Affected are GENESIS 11.03 and earlier; GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and IoTWorX 10.97.3 and earlier; and every version of MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz. ICONICS Suite and IoTWorX 10.98 and GENESIS 11.04 fix the main flaws; no fix is planned for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz. Mitsubishi reports no exploitation, and none of the CVEs is in KEV. CISA republished the advisory on 27 October as ICSA-26-300-02, scoring the two main flaws under CVSS v3.1 at 9.1 (CVE-2026-16438) and 8.1 (CVE-2026-16436). Our assessment: ICONICS software also runs building, energy and facility dashboards, so it can sit behind a terminal’s utility-plant or BMS views as well as on industrial plant.

items.title: October OT Patch Tuesday: unfixed critical web-server flaws across Siemens S7-1500 CPUs, and a Rockwell ArmorBlock I/O takeover bug
items.content_text: Siemens ProductCERT’s 13 October release, 17 advisories by SecurityWeek’s count, includes SSA-591731: eight web-server vulnerabilities in SIMATIC S7-1500, ET 200SP, ET 200pro and drive-controller CPUs, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6 and v4 9.4 by Siemens, that could let an attacker run code in an authorised user’s browser and carry out PLC operations with that user’s rights. All versions are affected and only mitigations exist so far. SSA-832641 fixes an authenticated path traversal in Industrial Edge devices (up to CVSS v3.1 9.1) for most models, but not yet for SCALANCE LPE9413/9433 or some HMI panels, and SSA-784472 lists 377 CVEs in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP module, also without a fix. Rockwell’s SD1801 covers 1732E ArmorBlock I/O modules at 3.012 and earlier: CVE-2026-12655 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) lets an unauthenticated attacker change the module’s web-server password and take it over, and CVE-2026-12656 is a network-storm denial of service that needs a power cycle to clear; 3.013 fixes both. None of these is in KEV or reported exploited. CISA republished the Siemens advisories on 22 October, and Siemens was still preparing fixes for the S7 web-server flaws. Our assessment: PLC families and distributed I/O like these are common in conveyor and materials-handling automation, so check whether the integrators behind your baggage and building systems use them rather than assuming either way.

items.title: CISA’s 1 October batch reaches terminal building systems: Armatura One access control ships an ActiveMQ flaw already exploited elsewhere, and Johnson Controls EasyIO building controllers get two fixes
items.content_text: CISA released six ICS advisories on 1 October, ICSA-26-274-01 to -06, and two cover building systems of the kind found in terminals. Armatura One, a physical access-control platform (-01), embeds a version of Apache ActiveMQ vulnerable to CVE-2023-46604, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 10.0. That flaw is already in CISA’s KEV catalog because it was exploited against other ActiveMQ deployments, including by ransomware actors; CISA reports no exploitation of Armatura One itself. The same advisory lists a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-94591) and hard-coded credentials (CVE-2026-94592), both 8.4 under v3.1 and 8.6 under v4, a log-exposure flaw (CVE-2026-94593, 7.8 and 8.5) and a lower-rated issue (CVE-2026-94594, 4.0). Versions before 4.7.2, and USA builds before 4.6.1, are affected; the fixes are 4.7.2 and 4.6.1_USA. CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors. Johnson Controls EasyIO Neo EC and CW building controllers (-04 and -05) have an information-exposure flaw, CVE-2026-64892 (3.5 under v3.1, 6.3 under v4), and cleartext transmission of sensitive data, CVE-2026-64893 (5.4 and 7.3), fixed in EC V3.3b64 and CW V3.3b26; CISA again lists Transportation Systems. The rest of the batch: Monta’s EV-charging platform (-02), whose missing authentication on a WebSocket channel, CVE-2026-95102 (9.4 under v3.1, 9.3 under v4), allows charging-station impersonation and has no fixed version, only configuration guidance — Monta points to OCPP 1.6 Security Profile 2 and says rate limiting is in place; ABB PCM600 up to 2.14 (-03), with a privilege-escalation and a path-traversal flaw, a workaround and no fixed version; and the Meari IoT cloud platform (-06), with no fix planned. CISA reports no known exploitation for any of the six. No airport is named. Our assessment: access control and building management are airport OT in everything but name, usually run by facilities and security contractors, and an access-control server with hard-coded keys and credentials is a direct route to doors, turnstiles and badge records. EV chargers appear in airport car parks and electric ground-support fleets, which is why the Monta item is listed here.

items.title: Moxa’s Remote Connect client can be tricked into trusting a fake server, and its end-of-life OnCell G3150A-LTE gateway has static keys and a command-injection flaw that will never be fixed
items.content_text: Moxa published advisory MPSA-269510 on 27 October. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, Moxa) affects the client of Moxa Remote Connect Suite, the OpenVPN-based tool engineers and integrators use to reach remote equipment: versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0 do not properly validate the server’s certificate, so an attacker on the network path could impersonate a trusted server and read or alter the session. Version 4.2.2 fixes it and is obtained through Moxa technical support. The same advisory covers the OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway, whose firmware carries static HTTPS and CA private keys (CVE-2026-111460, v4.0 7.7) and has an OS command injection in its SMS upgrade feature that needs high privileges and SMS management switched on (CVE-2026-111461, v4.0 7.5). The gateway is end-of-life and will not be fixed: Moxa’s mitigations are to reset the device so that it regenerates its keys and to keep SMS functions disabled, which is the default. No exploitation has been reported and none of the three CVEs is in KEV. Our assessment: remote-connect clients live on the laptops of the integrators who support baggage, BMS and airfield systems, and LTE gateways connect the edges of an airport estate — remote stands, fuel-farm telemetry, car parks and construction compounds — often without appearing in any inventory.

items.title: Fortinet has shipped fixes for FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator before saying what they fix — the details are due on 10 November
items.content_text: WaterISAC reported on 27 October that Fortinet has released coordinated security updates across five product lines and will publish the advisories, CVE IDs and CVSS scores on its PSIRT page on 10 November. The fixed releases it lists are FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14; FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13; FortiMail 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9, with 7.2 users moving to 7.4 or later; and FortiAuthenticator 8.0.4 and 6.6.11. FortiSASE was updated automatically and FortiManager Cloud may need a manual step. No exploitation of the newly fixed flaws has been reported. Until the CVEs are published, vulnerability scanners will not flag affected devices, so WaterISAC advises checking firmware versions directly, and it says Fortinet wants the upgrades treated as a priority change rather than routine maintenance. We found no public Fortinet post of its own, so these details rest on WaterISAC’s notice. The FortiMail releases also fix the exploited, KEV-listed CVE-2026-104286 (see that card). Our assessment: Fortinet firewalls and their managers are common on the boundary between airport or airline corporate networks and operational systems, and fixes that ship before their details give attackers time to compare old and new builds.

items.title: CISA republishes Siemens advisories for APOGEE, TALON and Desigo building controllers and WinCC — several of the affected models will never get a fix
items.content_text: On 22 October CISA republished Siemens’ 13 October ProductCERT advisories, and two concern the systems that run terminal buildings. ICSA-26-295-08 (Siemens SSA-333035) covers APOGEE, TALON and Desigo PXC/PXM automation stations. Four flaws in APOGEE and TALON controllers, an integer underflow (CVE-2026-102073, CVSS v3.1 8.2) and three stack-based buffer overflows in the FTP and web services (v3.1 7.5 each), let an unauthenticated attacker on the network read device memory or cause a denial of service. APOGEE PXC Compact and Modular and TALON TC controllers are fixed in V3.5.7 (BACnet) or V2.8.21 (P2 Ethernet), but APOGEE MBC and MEC controllers will not be fixed. Desigo PXC/PXM stations from V2.3 carry a lower-rated out-of-bounds read (CVE-2026-89208, v3.1 5.3), also with no fix planned. ICSA-26-295-13 (SSA-550198) covers SIMATIC WinCC: CVE-2026-59241 (v3.1 8.8) lets an authenticated user with database access escalate privileges and run commands on the host. WinCC V8.0 Update 11 and V8.1 Update 7 fix it; WinCC V7.5 has no fix. Both advisories list Transportation Systems, and neither reports exploitation. Our assessment: Siemens building automation is common in terminals, and controllers that will never be patched need a segmentation decision rather than a place on the patch list.

items.title: CISA’s 20 October batch lists Transportation Systems twice: a WAGO controller flaw that turns a low-privileged login into root, and PEAK PCAN driver crashes
items.content_text: CISA’s 20 October ICS batch includes two advisories that list Transportation Systems among the affected sectors. ICSA-26-293-02 republishes WAGO’s CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-096 for devices running WAGO OS Linux before firmware 4.10.0 (FW32): the CC100, PFC100 G2 and PFC200 G2 controllers, TP600 panels, the Edge Controller and WP400. In CVE-2026-80466 (CVSS v3.1 8.8) the web-based management’s routing settings do not validate input, so a remote user with a low-privileged account can store shell commands that a root helper script later runs. CVE-2026-88850 (v3.1 8.1) lets the same kind of account change root-owned PROFIBUS settings, including device addressing. Firmware 4.10.0 (FW32) fixes both, and custom firmware builds need WAGO support. ICSA-26-293-01 covers HMS Networks’ PEAK-System PCAN Windows CAN drivers up to 5.1.2: six flaws, the highest CVE-2026-103672 at v3.1 7.1, that a local user could use to crash Windows; CISA says they are not remotely exploitable, and 5.1.4 fixes them. CISA reports no exploitation of either, and CISA also lists Commercial Facilities for the WAGO devices. Our assessment: WAGO controllers are common in building, lighting and energy automation, and the WAGO flaw matters most where many people hold a low-privileged web login, as contractors and facilities staff often do.

items.title: Two CISA advisories that list Transportation Systems have no fix: hard-coded credentials in EseeCloud cameras and end-of-life EasyIO FG building controllers
items.content_text: CISA’s 15 October advisory ICSA-26-288-02 covers Guangzhou Juan IoT’s EseeCloud app (4.9.6 and earlier) and firmware (4.9.86.0 and earlier), used in low-cost IP cameras and video recorders: hard-coded credentials rated CVSS v3.1 9.8, plus two medium-severity flaws. The vendor did not respond to CISA and no fix exists. CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors using it, alongside energy, communications, financial services and government. On 6 October CISA republished Johnson Controls’ JCI-PSA-2026-12 as ICSA-26-279-01, covering EasyIO FG controller firmware: hard-coded credentials and improper privilege management, each CVSS v3.1 7.7. The product is end of life, no fix will be issued and Johnson Controls advises moving to EasyIO Neo R1; CISA notes high attack complexity and that the flaws are not remotely exploitable, and it again lists Transportation Systems. This is a different product from the EasyIO Neo controllers fixed in CISA’s 1 October batch. Neither advisory reports exploitation, and none of the CVEs is in KEV. Our assessment: cheap cameras and recorders reach airport estates through car-park, concession and contractor installations, and building controllers through facilities projects, so both are ownership problems before they are patching problems.

items.title: A signature-check flaw in Lantronix G520 cellular gateways could let an attacker replace the software and run code as root — the kind of box that connects an airport’s outlying sites
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-272-01 on 29 September for two flaws in Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateways running 2.6.0.4R6_stable: CVE-2026-91191, improper verification of a cryptographic signature, and CVE-2026-84409, a cross-site scripting flaw, each rated CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4 7.7. CISA says exploitation could allow an attacker to replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. The fix is release 2.6.0.7R6. CISA lists Transportation Systems, Energy, and Water and Wastewater as the sectors concerned and reports no known exploitation. No airport or airline is named. Our assessment of the aviation angle: cellular gateways are how sites without fixed lines get connected, and on an airport estate that tends to mean the edges — car-park pay stations and barriers, remote stands, fuel-farm and pump-station telemetry, construction compounds and contractor remote-support links — often installed by whoever built the site and missing from the network inventory. A gateway that accepts replaced software is a persistent foothold at exactly the places least watched.

items.title: CISA’s 2030 strategy puts operational technology and consequence-based priorities at the centre — a review of its core services starts within 60 days
items.content_text: CISA released “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail” on 26 October. Acting Director Nick Andersen says the agency will move from passive defence to an aggressive, anticipatory stance that removes adversary footholds, with resilience as the foundation. The plan commits CISA to helping operators improve OT security, including asset visibility and intrusion detection; to producing data-driven guidance on third-party and supply-chain dependencies; and to helping sectors focus resources where they have the greatest impact, including through a national risk register on the UK model. It sets three timelines: a review of core services and capabilities beginning within 60 days, an implementation plan with success metrics within 180 days, and a progress update after a year. It places no new obligations on operators, and Cybersecurity Dive notes that it does not address the agency’s shrinking field presence after workforce cuts. Aviation is not named. For airports and airlines the relevance is direction of travel: federal attention and services are being steered toward OT visibility, detection and the most consequential assets, the same case that terminal and airfield OT programmes make internally.

items.title: The FCC blocks its first devices under the covered-component rule: a wireless video transmitter and a dashcam built on Huawei’s HiSilicon surveillance chips
items.content_text: On 22 October the FCC barred two devices, a wireless video transmitter and a dashboard camera, from the US market because both use chips from HiSilicon, a Huawei subsidiary on the FCC’s Covered List that markets the chips for surveillance use. They are the first bans under rules that took effect on 13 October and prohibit devices containing smart components from Covered List companies; before then the FCC did not ban otherwise lawful devices simply for containing such parts. Chairman Brendan Carr called video devices with surveillance chips from Covered List entities “an obvious and unacceptable risk”. The Record does not name the device makers. A separate FCC vote on withdrawing recognition from test labs in countries without mutual-recognition agreements, China among them, was set for 29 October; its outcome is pending. This is a procurement and supply-chain rule, not a reported attack. Our assessment: airports buy large numbers of cameras, video encoders and vehicle cameras, usually through security and fleet contractors, so chip provenance belongs on the purchasing checklist.

items.title: GAO finds only 7 of 22 civilian agencies fully meet federal rules for managing networked IoT and OT devices — and an industry coalition now asks CISA for a binding OT directive
items.content_text: GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September, reviewed how 22 civilian CFO Act agencies manage networked Internet of Things and OT devices against OMB requirements that date from December 2023, were updated in January 2025 and carried a September 2024 completion deadline. Fifteen agencies had established device inventories, 11 maintained them, 10 included all the required information, and only seven fully met all three requirements. No agency reported an IoT cybersecurity waiver. GAO notes that OMB has not issued updated guidance covering fiscal year 2026 and makes one recommendation: that OMB issue updated guidance covering networked IoT and OT devices and oversee its implementation. On 6 October CyberScoop reported that the OT Cybersecurity Coalition is urging CISA to issue a binding operational directive focused solely on OT security at federal agencies, citing the GAO findings and this summer’s water-utility attacks. The coalition wants an accountable OT cybersecurity officer at each agency, minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, alignment with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and a review of whether NSA’s OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. This is a proposal only. CISA has announced no directive and did not respond to CyberScoop. For aviation readers the relevance is indirect. GAO’s numbers show how hard it is to keep even an inventory of networked devices current, which is the same first step airport OT programmes struggle with, and a federal OT directive, if one were issued, would become a public reference point for what a minimum OT programme looks like.

items.title: CISA’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month campaign, “Securing the Next 250”, asks operators to reduce, replace and recover — and replacing end-of-support kit is the hard part for airport OT
items.content_text: CISA launched “Securing the Next 250” at the start of Cybersecurity Awareness Month, as reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. The campaign frames its advice for organisations as three Rs: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, and recover quickly to keep operations running. For individuals it repeats four practices: avoid and report phishing, use strong passwords, use multifactor authentication with a password manager, and keep software updated. Acting Director Nick Andersen tied the campaign to the knock-on effect of disruption: when critical infrastructure fails, the businesses and communities that depend on it fail with it. It is a voluntary awareness campaign, not a rule or directive, and it sets no sector-specific requirement. For airports the useful part is the middle R. Terminal OT often includes devices past their support life — ageing BMS front ends, baggage-control workstations, access-control servers and controllers fitted at construction — and replacing them runs on capital-project timescales, not patch cycles.

items.title: GAO’s industry panel says overlapping federal cyber-reporting rules can pull responders away from the incident — and the CIRCIA final rule has reached White House review
items.content_text: The Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-109197, “Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them”, on 28 September. It reports a virtual panel held on 16 July with six industry representatives from energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health. Panelists said it could be hard to meet every reporting requirement while also remediating a cyber threat, saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector rules, and half of them agreed that progress on harmonisation had been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency such as CISA to coordinate reporting; and closer government–industry collaboration. The report makes no formal recommendations, and transportation was not on the panel. Separately, CISA has sent its final rule under the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, which logged it for review on 1 October; the text is not public, and as of 28 October we found no report that the rule has been published. The statutory deadline was October 2025 and CISA’s later targets of May and September 2026 slipped; HIPAA Journal reports publication is expected before the end of the year, and the text can still change in review. Once in force it would require covered incidents to be reported within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours; any text quoted today as the rule is the 2024 proposal. For aviation the relevance is practical: airports, airlines and their service providers can answer to several regulators for the same incident, and the harmonisation question the panel raised is the one an incident team meets in its first hours.
